title: Curios of the Week #179
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman's weekly roundup (issue #179, partially paywalled) covers education research news, teacher standards, and current events. The featured discussion centers on Australia's Professional Standards for Teachers review, in which the Australian Association for Research in Education (AARE) has been campaigning to steer submissions toward endorsing experiential and embodied learning approaches. Ashman critiques a blog post by Curtin University's Kelly Ilich that advocates rewriting the 'know the content and how to teach it' standard to include movement, experimentation, and observation—approaches he argues lack support from the same OECD evidence base the author cites. Ashman acknowledges a limited role for experiential learning but warns against including it in professional standards without careful qualification about when it is appropriate. The issue also previews a new podcast episode ('When Will They Learn? Episode #14') and introduces a 'Police State of the Week' segment on civil liberties concerns in Britain. The full issue's 'Curios' (linked articles on cognitive load theory and mathematics misconceptions) are behind a subscriber paywall.
points: The AARE is actively lobbying to influence Australia's teacher standards review toward experiential and embodied learning methods, despite weak empirical support—Ashman sees this as education academics prioritizing preferred ideology over evidence.

Ashman distinguishes legitimate uses of experiential learning (developing 'biologically primary' knowledge or deepening expertise in those who already have domain knowledge) from inappropriate uses as a general instructional default.
The OECD is cited by the AARE to endorse experiential learning, even as Ashman argues the OECD's own research repeatedly contradicts that endorsement.
The full issue previews content on 'a pivot in cognitive load theory' and 'mathematics teaching misconceptions'—topics central to evidence-based instruction—though these sections are paywalled.
Ashman co-hosts the 'When Will They Learn?' podcast, with episode #14 covering Australian teacher standards and Daisy Christodoulou's work on transferable skills.
quotes: This week's Curios include a pivot in cognitive load theory, some mathematics teaching misconceptions, an authoritarian police state and much more.

Students do not learn only by receiving explanations or interacting with text on a screen. They learn through movement, experimentation, conversation, observation, making and participation in shared physical and social environments.

The OECD identifies teacher-guided and experiential learning as foundations of active learning for human flourishing. Teachers create the conditions in which students investigate, encounter uncertainty, revise their thinking and connect abstract ideas to lived experience. The Castlereagh Statement similarly affirms the importance of embodied experiences, human educators and community.
The OECD really should know better by now, given that its own evidence keeps proving it wrong.

Yes, there is a role for experiential learning in schools, but that is either for developing 'biologically primary' knowledge—see more on this below—rather than the typical content of the school curriculum, or, depending on what you mean by experiential learning, for developing further expertise in individuals who already have lots of relevant knowledge. Unless this is made clear, experiential learning should stay out of the Standards.

There have been mutterings from right-wing and, especially, American accounts on Twitter/X that all is not right in Britain. It is hard to take these too seriously because I have visited the place while others have been voicing these concerns and nothing seems particularly amiss.
